Mining · Rwanda

Land change in and around your mining licence area in Rwanda

Dated maps of the pits, excavations, spoil, cleared ground, tracks, tailings and rehabilitated land in and around your licence area, with the river and wetland buffers in RMB’s guidelines checked and change flagged between surveys. For licence holders working tin, tantalum, lithium, gold, gemstones and other minerals under Law n° 072/2024. Satellite first, and a person reviews every result before it reaches you.

Send us your licence area See sample outputs

The problem, in your words

Small licence blocks, busy ground

“New pits keep opening near our block.”

RMB’s investment prospectus (October 2025) describes a sector moving towards “professionalization and industrialization”, and licence holders need to know what is changing on and around their ground. Excavations just outside a licence area are where questions start, and a dated map is where the answers begin.

“RMB wants the rivers and wetlands kept clear.”

RMB’s 2026 environmental and social guidelines say “Mining is not permitted within 20 meters of wetlands, 10 meters of main rivers, and 5 meters from the banks of smaller rivers”. A dated map shows where the ground inside those distances has changed.

“We have to show the land is being restored.”

Reclamation, re-vegetation, mine closure and rehabilitation are named among the essential services in RMB’s 2019 service regulations, and RMB’s 2026 guidelines point to “remote sensing for deforestation monitoring”. Evidence is needed between dates, not only at closure.

“Our tailings need watching.”

The guidelines describe satellite imagery and aerial surveys as tools for following land-use change around tailings facilities over time, with routine inspections “supplemented by drone surveys”. An RMB project note on the sector adds that low use of modern technology leaves “a big percentage of minerals unrecovered in tailings”.

Who this is for

  • Licence holders and mine managers
  • Environment and rehabilitation officers
  • Community and District liaison teams
  • ESIA consultants
  • Investors’ and lenders’ due-diligence teams
  • GIS and survey teams, as users

The law

What Law n° 072/2024 sets for the land

A summary of the public rules, last reviewed 27 September 2026, for orientation. It is not legal advice; the sources are linked.

Law n° 072/2024 of 26/06/2024 on mining and quarry operations (loi portant exploitation des mines et carrières; Kinyarwanda itegeko rigenga ubucukuzi bw’amabuye y’agaciro na kariyeri) repealed Law n° 58/2018; licences granted under the old law stay valid until they expire (arts. 75, 77). Its licence types are exploration, small-, medium- and large-scale mining, mineral trading and mineral processing (art. 7), and a mining licence is an uruhushya rw’ubucukuzi bw’amabuye y’agaciro. RMB’s investment prospectus (October 2025) presents a portfolio of tantalum, tin, lithium, gold, gemstones, industrial minerals and beryllium, and lists tungsten refining, lithium processing and beryl beneficiation among the value-addition opportunities.

Ownership
Minerals are vested in the State “notwithstanding personal ownership of land” (art. 3)
Compensation first
Fair compensation to the landowner or lawful occupier before mining, after which the land is registered to the State (art. 4)
Maximum block sizes
Exploration 400 ha, small-scale 50 ha, medium-scale 100 ha, large-scale 400 ha (art. 8)
Terms
Exploration up to 4 years and mining up to 15 years at first (art. 13)
Beacons
The holder installs “beacons around the mining licence area” (art. 24(c))
Records
The holder keeps “aerial photographs” and other data at an address in Rwanda (art. 24(d)(ii))

Applications go through the One Stop Center (art. 9), potential mining areas are demarcated with their names and geographic coordinates (art. 5), and each holder agrees a development and social-welfare plan with the District (art. 74). Tailings are managed as regulations provide, and damage to land and property is fairly compensated (art. 24(i)–(j)). Licences are administered by the Rwanda Mines, Petroleum and Gas Board (RMB) through the GIMCS mining cadastre.

What we map

The ground in and around your licence area, between dates

Excavations and pits

Pits, trenches, water-filled excavations and disturbed ground, with new sites flagged between dates and confirmed by a reviewer.

Spoil, tailings and stockpiles

Spoil heaps, tailings areas, stockpiles and laydown areas, and how their footprint changes.

Cleared ground and tracks

New clearings and access tracks into and around the licence area. Tracks under tree canopy can be missed.

Structures

Structures inside the licence area and in a ring around it, for compensation, relocation and engagement planning.

River and wetland buffers

We buffer the river and wetland lines you work to at 20 m for wetlands, 10 m for main rivers and 5 m for the banks of smaller rivers, the distances in RMB’s 2026 guidelines, and list each excavation, clearing and structure inside them with its distance and the imagery date. The environment law sets its own distances for other activities, such as nothing built in a swamp or its 20 m buffer (Law n° 48/2018, art. 49), and we can add those bands too.

Around the boundary

Excavations near the licence area

Licence blocks in Rwanda are small: the law caps small-scale mining at 50 ha and medium-scale at 100 ha, so the land just outside the beacons matters as much as the land inside. We map the licence area and a ring around it at the width you choose, and flag new pits, spoil, clearings and tracks between surveys, each with its distance to your boundary.

Whether an excavation near your licence area is authorised is for you and RMB to establish. We describe the ground, never the people, and what you do with a flagged site is your decision. In the rainy season, radar comparisons show larger ground changes even under cloud, and flagged areas are followed up with optical imagery or a drone check.

What a flag is

An indication for your team to check, located and dated, with before-and-after views. It is not proof of who did anything, and it will not catch every change: small or covered workings can be missed.

Excavation and ground-disturbance mapping

Tailings and rehabilitation

Dated evidence that the land is recovering

Tailings footprint

The outline of tailings areas and the ground around them compared between dated surveys, with any new structures or clearings nearby listed. It is land-use change, not a measure of ground movement or dam stability.

Revegetation

Vegetation cover on rehabilitated land and closed pits compared between dates, from Copernicus Sentinel data and, where flown, drone surveys. It shows the trend; it is not an ecological assessment.

Tree-cover loss

Regular notices of tree-cover loss and ground disturbance near your licence area from global satellite alert systems such as Global Forest Watch, checked by our team. Alerts are indications to check, not proof.

RMB’s 2026 guidelines record that “The government of Rwanda urges mining companies to shift from artisanal to mechanized mineral processing technologies”, and its prospectus names “drones and geospatial mapping” among smart-mining technologies.

Vegetation, land cover and fire

Expansion and compensation

Record the land before the next pit

Law n° 072/2024 requires fair compensation before mining starts (art. 4) and for damage to land and property (art. 24(j)). The expropriation law also counts “minerals and other natural resources in the public domain” among activities of public interest (Law n° 32/2015, art. 5), and all works related to mining are on the list of projects that need an environmental impact assessment (Ministerial Order of 2018, Annex I).

Before an expansion, we produce a dated register of the structures and cleared land in the new footprint, with imagery, coordinates and IDs. It supports your valuation, your compensation records and, where a lender applies them, cut-off-date records under IFC Performance Standard 5. It does not replace the census or the asset inventory, and it never establishes ownership, use or value.

For the footprint

  • Structures and cleared land, dated and located
  • New features after the record date, flagged and confirmed
  • A land-use and land-cover baseline around the site
  • The imagery history of disputed parcels

Resettlement cut-off-date baselines

Working on a licence area

RMB’s rules for service providers

RMB Regulations N° 002/MINES/RMB/2019 of 18/07/2019 list as essential services “mineral or quarry exploration services, including geological, geophysics, remote sensing and geochemistry activities” and “environmental and social management services such as reclamation, re-vegetation, mine waste and water and tailings management, mine closure and rehabilitation” (art. 4). A licence holder “must not engage or employ” a mining or quarry services provider unless the provider holds an RMB licence or registration (art. 5). RMB decides an application within 60 days (art. 13) and issues the licence for five years, renewable (art. 14).

RMB still lists these regulations, and publishes its lists of providers holding service licences on its guidelines page. Law n° 072/2024 provides for regulations on private mining and quarry services (art. 71), and asks licence holders to give preference to Rwandan contractors “provided that the rates, quality and time schedule for delivery are competitive” (art. 72).

Before work starts

Ask any provider, including us, how the art. 5 requirement is met for your contract. Every AfriScan proposal for work on a Rwandan licence area sets it out.

Drones on a mine site

Satellite first, drones where they add detail

Part 27 sets no drone rule specific to mines. A flight over a licence area is a commercial Specific operation with registration, a pilot licence and an activity permit (and, where RCAA asks for one, a UAS Operator Certificate), the consent of occupiers where the flight passes over their property or near people, and care around blasting areas, which are hazards. Drone surveys are subject to the RCAA approvals, security reviews and consents each job requires, so a survey starts from satellite imagery and adds drone orthophotos and elevation models where they add detail.

How it works

From licence area to reviewed map

  1. Scope

    You send the licence-area coordinates, the river and wetland lines you work to and what the maps are for. We agree the bands, imagery and deliverables in a written proposal.

  2. Screen from satellite

    Dated satellite imagery and open datasets give the first map of excavations, clearings, tracks, tailings and structures.

  3. Review and flag

    A reviewer confirms, corrects and adds features, and marks new sites since the last survey.

  4. Deliver and repeat

    A PDF report in English and GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers go to the contacts you name. Re-surveys follow the schedule you set.

Honest scope

What we do, and what we don’t

What we do

  • Map excavations, spoil, tailings, cleared ground, tracks and structures visible from the air
  • Check the 20 m, 10 m and 5 m river and wetland buffers
  • Flag change between dated surveys, confirmed by a reviewer
  • Track revegetation on rehabilitated land

What we don’t do

  • Exploration, geology or resource estimates
  • See underground workings, or measure ground movement
  • Identify, count or follow people
  • Verify title or beacons, or decide whether an excavation is authorised
  • Offer field or drone work within 10 km of the DRC border

Frequently asked questions

Can you tell us who is digging near our licence area?

No. We map the ground, such as pits, spoil heaps, water-filled excavations, cleared ground and new tracks, with new sites flagged between dates and confirmed by a reviewer. We never identify, count or follow people. Whether an excavation near your licence area is authorised is for you and RMB to establish.

Can you check the 20 m, 10 m and 5 m buffers?

Yes. RMB’s 2026 guidelines say mining is not permitted within 20 m of wetlands, 10 m of main rivers and 5 m of the banks of smaller rivers. Send the river and wetland lines you work to, or tell us which ones to use, and we list the excavations, cleared ground and structures inside each buffer, with the imagery date on every record.

Does a provider need an RMB licence to work on our licence area?

RMB’s 2019 regulations say a mining licence holder “must not engage or employ” a mining or quarry services provider unless the provider holds an RMB licence or registration (art. 5), and they list remote sensing among the essential services. Ask any provider, including us, how that requirement is met for your contract before work starts; our proposal sets it out.

Can you see underground workings or shafts?

No. Underground workings, and shafts under cover, are not visible from above. We map what shows at the surface.

Can you confirm our licence boundary or beacons?

No. We work from the licence-area coordinates you give us, from your licence or the GIMCS mining cadastre, and we do not verify title or tenure. Beacons are yours to install under art. 24(c) of the mining law, and a boundary that needs surveying is a land surveyor’s work.

Can your maps stand as our rehabilitation or closure report?

They support it. Revegetation trends and earthworks between dates give you dated evidence for your environmental and closure reporting. They are not an ecological assessment, a closure certificate or a sign-off by RMB.

The mining law asks us to keep aerial photographs in Rwanda. How do your files fit?

Art. 24(d)(ii) of Law n° 072/2024 asks licence holders to keep “aerial photographs” and other data at an address in Rwanda. Everything we deliver is a set of files handed to you, the PDF report, the GIS layers and, where the imagery licence allows, the imagery itself, so you can keep them with the rest of your licence records.

Send us your licence area

Licence-area coordinates or a boundary file (Shapefile, GeoPackage, KML or GeoJSON), the District, the mineral and the licence type, and what the maps are for: buffers, tailings, rehabilitation or an expansion. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
